name: Vilvanatheswarar Temple, Thiruvalam
deity: Shiva as Vilvanatheswarar, with the goddess Valli Nayaki
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Thondai Nadu, sung in the Tevaram; structural temple with 8th-century Pallava inscriptions and later additions
dynasty: Pallava (Nandivarman II era) and later Tamil patrons
summary: Vilvanatheswarar is the Shiva temple of Thiruvalam in the Thondai country, a Paadal Petra Sthalam grown around a self-formed linga in what tradition remembers as an ancient bilva forest, and known for some of the earliest inscriptions to name the Tevaram singers.

sections.history: Thiruvalam, called Thiruvallam in the Tevaram, stands in the Thondai country near Vellore, on the plain watered by the Ponnai river. The presiding Lord is praised in the hymns of the child-saint Sambandar, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam, one of the temples sung by the Tamil Shaiva saints. The shrine is valued by historians for its stone record: its north wall carries one of the earliest inscriptions to name the singers of the Tevaram, and the temple preserves grants from the 8th-century Pallava king Nandivarman II and from later dynasties. Raised and enlarged in stone across the centuries, it has been kept in worship without a break.
sections.architecture: Built in the Dravidian manner and entered through a gopuram, the temple holds the Shiva linga as Vilvanatheswarar in its sanctum, believed to have arisen of itself from a termite mound. The goddess Valli Nayaki is honoured in her own shrine. The outer faces of the sanctum carry the koshta murtis, the attendant forms of Vinayaka, Dakshinamurti, Vishnu and Brahma, set as guardians of the directions. The temple's sacred tree is the bilva, the leaf dear to Shiva, and sources differ on the exact number of gopuram tiers and the size of the enclosure.
sections.legends: Tradition remembers the place as a forest of bilva trees, where a cow of its own accord would daily shed its milk over an anthill; the mound was found to hold a linga, and the temple grew around it. A second story tells of a devotee troubled by a giant who seized the water he drew each day; he prayed to the Lord of Thiruvalam, and Shiva sent his bull Nandi to stand guard over him. Told as local tradition rather than firm history, these tales carry the shrine's sense of a sanctuary raised where the sacred first showed itself.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the festivals common to the great Shiva shrines, with a car festival and street processions drawing the deities through the village, and Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham observed with devotion. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally; a visit near a festival finds the old shrine at its most alive.
sections.experience: Thiruvalam rewards a slow visit. Come to the sanctum of Vilvanatheswarar, turn to the goddess Valli Nayaki in her shrine, and look to the sculpted guardian forms on the sanctum walls. Those drawn to history will want to read the early inscriptions on the temple's stone, among the oldest to name the Tevaram saints, a reminder that the hymns sung here were already old when the walls were carved. The river plain spreads beyond the walls, and within them the temple keeps the quiet of a very old sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvalam is a village in Vellore district, about 2 km from Tiruvalam railway station on the Chennai–Katpadi line, and close to the Chennai–Bangalore highway roughly 10 km from Ranipet. Vellore and Katpadi are the nearest large centres, with frequent buses; confirm distances and connections locally.
